extracted.intended_audience: civic-minded readers, students of political theory, journalists, and members of the public interested in how publics judge rules and social problems
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and heuristics for how members of a public should recognize social problems, judge the defectiveness of rules, identify legitimate spokesmen, and decide when and how the public ought to intervene or deliberate. Focuses on tests of assent, conformity, representation, and the public's proper scope of concern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem as altered relationship between variables
rubrics_metrics.description: A problem is the result of change that alters the relationship between two dependent variables; change by itself is not a problem unless measured against another element that does not change at the same pace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Malthus’s population/food example illustrates that population growth is a problem only when food supply does not keep pace; the automobile is a problem in cities because automobiles increase faster than street width, competent drivers, police capacity, etc. Anti-pattern: Calling any change a problem without identifying the disturbed relationship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Change is significant only in relation to something else
rubrics_metrics.description: Change would be unnoticeable unless measured against some other element which does not change at the same pace; therefore determine the relevant comparator before declaring a problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: look for the paired variable(s) (e.g., supply vs demand, vehicles vs street capacity) whose mismatch produces the felt difficulty. Avoid treating isolated statistics (e.g., 'many automobiles') as sufficient evidence of a problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic problems as maladjustment of wants and limited means
rubrics_metrics.description: Economic problems arise from the disharmony between human wants and means of satisfying them when those means are available only in limited quantity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Solution methods (per Cassel): (1) eliminate less important wants (restrict demand), (2) better use the means available, (3) increase personal exertion (increase supply). Use these as mutually exclusive families of remedies depending on feasibility and preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public interest limited to the method and enforcement of rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The public’s interest is not in particular laws or customs but in the maintenance of a régime of rules, contracts, and customs — i.e., the method of law, enforcement, and revision rather than substantive prescriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: The public should prioritize that rules be enforceable and that there be settled procedures for changing unenforceable rules. Anti-pattern: The public attempting to decide fine-grained substantive disputes (which invites capture by special interests).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two tests the public must ask about any contested rule
rubrics_metrics.description: When confronting a disputed rule the public should ask: (1) Is the rule defective? and (2) Which agency is most likely to mend it?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the quick, objective tests usable by someone who lacks deep subject-matter understanding. The public need not and should not attempt to resolve technical merits; instead it should use these tests to decide whether and how to intervene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test of assent for legitimate rule-change
rubrics_metrics.description: A new rule cannot be expected to work unless it has been first understood and approved by those who must live according to it; violation of a rule without seeking assent is an attack on its validity except in genuine emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If innovation occurs without assent and no emergency justification exists, public condemnation is warranted. Exceptions: exceptional times or exceptional actors may justify breaking the rule, but such exceptions must justify themselves; otherwise the dogma that assent is necessary holds to prevent anarchy of personal rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting lack of assent via protest and nonconformity
rubrics_metrics.description: Assent is lacking when there is open protest or widespread refusal to conform; a workable rule will not evoke much protest or disobedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When many persons are involved, protests become a public matter; where few are involved, the public best refrains. The public should measure significance of protest by whether spokesmen are authorized and whether nonconformity is widespread enough to threaten peaceful adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule-of-thumb for recognizing authorized spokesmen
rubrics_metrics.description: In general the public should accept as authorized the apparent leaders who bear the external signs of office (officials, elected leaders) unless there is clear evidence of rebellion or challenge to their credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof lies on those who deny the spokesman’s authority. For nations, unless there is open rebellion, public opinion must treat the government in office as committed. Anti-pattern: Playing politics inside another’s frontiers by refusing to recognize de facto officials without clear cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weighing assent in presence of internal opposition
rubrics_metrics.description: If spokesmen are elected their assent can be treated as reliable until a new election; if they are not elective and a rebellious opposition exists, their assent is only tentative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The public should use these practical criteria to limit what settlements are reasonable in face of opposition; do not attempt fine-grained adjudication of internal challenges but use leadership legitimacy and evidence of rebellion as modifiers of assent's weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conformity as a symptom of rule functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: A rule that is repeatedly broken or widely criticized is defective because it does not define conduct that can normally be expected of those under it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Widespread criticism is not merely intellectual dissent but often signals practical evasion—both are evidence the rule is unstable. The public can use the frequency of breaches and criticism as a heuristic that the rule 'does not work.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Public intervention threshold: scale and tribunal-impugnment
rubrics_metrics.description: The public need deal only with failures: customs accepted by all, contracts carried out, or rules enforced raise no public question; public intervention is warranted when many people are involved or when public tribunals themselves are impugned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For disputes involving very few persons, defer to appropriate tribunals and checks; the public is not equipped for minutiae. When large groups are embroiled or the legitimacy of adjudicating bodies is questioned, the public should take an interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detecting and discounting self-interested groups
rubrics_metrics.description: The public must detect and discount spurious members—self-interested groups that pretend to be the public—because they confuse the public point of view and can produce false adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The main practical defense is insistence on open debate: free discussion tends to betray partisans and exposes who genuinely represents which interest. The purpose is not to stigmatize private interest but to prevent counterfeit strength from misleading the public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of open public debate to expose partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Insisting on full freedom of discussion is essential because advocates are likely to expose one another; open debate helps identify partisan actors who seek to pose as the disinterested public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if debate yields no decisive conclusion, it serves to reveal who is an advocate and who is a disinterested spokesman, enabling bystanders to make informed choices about whether to join a partisan cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public's proper role as reserve force for enforcement not maker of substance
rubrics_metrics.description: The public should act as a reserve force that supports the method and spirit of law and morals — i.e., enforcement and predictability — rather than attempting to prescribe substantive rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the public should mobilize its power (votes, criticism, boycotts) to reinforce agencies that enforce workable rules or to back plausible reforms of method; avoid trying to determine the substantive balance among competing special interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessing solutions by possible adaptations before declaring problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Before labeling a condition a problem, consider whether shifts in behavior or technological/social adjustments (e.g., people eating less, birth control, increased food supply) might remove the imbalance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use counterfactual reasoning: show how changes in either variable could avert the problem to avoid premature policy action. Anti-pattern: policy responses that ignore potential spontaneous or technological adjustments.
